nodes.title: MCG-finite representations
nodes.statement: For an oriented connected finite-type surface S=Σ(g,n), a rank-r complex representation ρ is MCG-finite when its actual GL_r(C)-conjugacy class has finite orbit under orientation-preserving mapping classes acting through Out(π₁S). Use pure mapping classes for ordered punctures; full versus pure finiteness is equivalent because their index is finite. No semisimplification is taken.
proofSteps: Use conjugacy of homomorphisms as an equivalence relation; precomposition by an inner automorphism induces conjugation by ρ of that element.
Descend the outer action to classes; identify finite orbits with finite-index stabilizers.
acceptance: Agrees with HasFiniteConjugacyOrbitUnder of the suggested file for the based action of PMod(g,n+1) on π₁(Σ(g,n),x); inner automorphisms act by conjugation of ρ, so the based and outer formulations give the same predicate.
The predicate is unchanged when Mod(g,n) is replaced by PMod(g,n) or by any finite-index subgroup.

sources.match: Definition 1.1.1 calls ρ MCG-finite when its conjugacy class has finite orbit under the outer action of Mod(g,n), and the following paragraph stresses actual conjugacy classes rather than points of the character variety; §2.1 develops basic properties.

The input is finite orbit of possibly nonsplit representations.

nodes.title: Punctured versal families
nodes.statement: A punctured étale-versal (g,n)-family is a smooth proper connected genus-g curve C→M over a connected smooth complex variety, with n ordered disjoint sections, whose classifying map M→M(g,n) is dominant and étale; C° is the complement of those sections. In family arguments impose 2g−2+n>0. The word versal here includes étaleness.
proofSteps: Import the common pointed-curve moduli carrier, not a second moduli stack.
Define the open complement and the dominant étale condition on the supplied classifying map.
acceptance: For (g,n)=(0,3), M(0,3) is a point: a versal family is a finite étale cover of a point carrying the constant family P¹ with three sections, and the punctured fibre group is free of rank two.
A dominant classifying map that is ramified (for instance a ramified double cover of a level chart) is excluded: versal includes étale.

sources.match: Notation 1.10.1 defines families of n-pointed curves in the hyperbolic range, calls them versal when the classifying map to M(g,n) is dominant and étale, and introduces the punctured family; §1.3 drops étaleness, the misprint PAPER-LANDESMAN-LITT-24/E3. Lemmas 2.1.4–2.1.5 are the first uses.

nodes.title: Moduli and point-pushing comparison
nodes.statement: For 2g−2+n>0, the analytic orbifold fundamental group of the ordered moduli stack M(g,n) is PMod(g,n); that of its universal punctured curve M(g,n+1) is PMod(g,n+1). The fibre inclusion is point pushing and its conjugation action agrees with the surface outer action. These are orbifold groups, not the fundamental groups of coarse spaces.
proofSteps: Apply C.0/teichmuller-uniformization to M(g,n) and M(g,n+1); the latter is the smooth punctured universal curve over the former (MC.2 interface).

Compare the homotopy sequence of the forgetful map with the Birman exact sequence (LV.5/birman-exact-sequence): the fibre inclusion is point pushing (LV.5/point-push), and conjugation by lifts induces the surface outer action.
Check the path-composition convention against TauCeti.LocalCoefficientSystem.monodromyRepresentation before identifying left and right actions.
acceptance: For (g,n)=(0,3) the forgetful map M(0,4)→M(0,3) is the thrice-punctured line over a point, and the Birman sequence becomes π₁(Σ(0,3))≅PMod(0,4)≅F₂ with PMod(0,3) trivial.
Changing the chosen marking changes both vertical isomorphisms by the same inner automorphism, so the comparison diagram commutes for every choice.

sources.match: Lemma 2.0.1 identifies π₁(M(g,n)) with PMod(g,n) and π₁(M(g,n+1)) with PMod(g,n+1), compatibly with the forgetful map and the Birman sequence, up to the choice of marking; the second identification is printed as PMod(g,n) (source issue E1).

nodes.title: Teichmüller uniformization of the pointed moduli stack
nodes.statement: For 2g−2+n>0, Teichmüller space T(g,n) of marked complex structures on Σ(g,n) is a contractible complex manifold of dimension 3g−3+n. PMod(g,n) acts on it by change of marking, properly discontinuously with finite stabilizers (the automorphism groups of the pointed curves), and the analytic stack M(g,n)^an is the orbifold quotient [T(g,n)/PMod(g,n)]. The universal pointed curve pulled back to T(g,n) is topologically the trivial family T(g,n)×Σ(g,n) with its n constant sections. Hence M(g,n)^an has contractible orbifold universal cover and orbifold fundamental group PMod(g,n); changing the marking of the base fibre changes this identification by an inner automorphism.
proofSteps: Teichmüller’s theorem identifies T(g,n) with an open ball of real dimension 6g−6+2n; this is the recorded Teichmüller gap (Farb–Margalit, Primer, Chapters 10–12, is the intended source and was not read here).

Proper discontinuity and the stabilizer computation follow from the same theory; the quotient is the analytic moduli stack by the universal property of the moduli pseudofunctor applied to the universal marked family.

A properly discontinuous action on a contractible space identifies the orbifold fundamental group of the quotient with the acting group, up to the inner automorphism fixed by the chosen base point and marking.
acceptance: For (g,n)=(0,4): M(0,4) is the thrice-punctured line, a scheme with no stabilizers, and the theorem gives π₁ ≅ PMod(0,4), a free group of rank two (LL24 uses this freeness after Question 10.1.1, p.49).

For (g,n)=(1,1): T(1,1) is the upper half-plane, PMod(1,1)=SL₂(Z) acts through PSL₂(Z) with −1 acting trivially, and the generic stabilizer ±1 is the elliptic involution; the coarse quotient is the j-line but the orbifold group is SL₂(Z), not PSL₂(Z).
The theorem is about the stack: the coarse space of M(g,n) has a different fundamental group whenever stabilizers are nontrivial.

sources.locator: Proof of Lemma 2.0.1, p.12; proof of Lemma 2.1.5, p.14
sources.match: The proof of Lemma 2.0.1 derives π₁(M(g,n))≅PMod(g,n) from contractibility of the universal cover of M(g,n) and the properly discontinuous PMod action, citing Farb–Margalit §10.6.3 and p.353; Lemma 2.1.5 uses the same contractibility for injectivity of the fibre group. This node states that input; its own proof is the recorded Teichmüller gap.

nodes.title: Versal family fundamental groups
nodes.statement: For a punctured étale-versal hyperbolic family and compatible basepoints, 1→π₁(C°_m)→π₁(C°)→π₁(M)→1 is exact; the map π₁(M)→PMod(g,n) has finite-index image. Consequently the outer monodromy on the fibre is the restriction of the mapping-class action.
proofSteps: Finite index: after pulling back to a finite étale scheme cover of M(g,n) (a fine level chart), the image of π₁ of a dominant étale source has finite index; this uses the theorem that a dominant morphism of normal complex varieties has finite-index image on fundamental groups (recorded finite-index gap; LL24 cites Debarre Lemma 4.19).

The punctured family is a locally trivial fibre bundle by the relative Ehresmann theorem for a proper submersion with disjoint sections (recorded Ehresmann gap), so its homotopy sequence is exact except possibly on the left.

Injectivity on the left: the fibre inclusion factors through the universal punctured curve, where the fibre group injects because the orbifold universal cover of M(g,n) is contractible (C.0/teichmuller-uniformization). Do not assume π₂(M)=0.
acceptance: For the constant family over a point with (g,n)=(0,3) the sequence is 1→F₂→F₂→1→1.
The finite-index assertion needs dominance: a constant map from a point has trivial image, of infinite index in PMod(g,n) when 3g−3+n>0.

sources.match: Lemma 2.1.4 shows the image of π₁(M) in PMod(g,n) has finite index for dominant étale M→M(g,n), via a finite étale scheme cover and Debarre Lemma 4.19; Lemma 2.1.5 proves exactness of the fibre sequence, deducing injectivity from the universal punctured curve.

nodes.title: Fibral finite-orbit monodromy
nodes.statement: The restriction to a fibre of every finite-dimensional complex local system on the total space of a punctured étale-versal hyperbolic family is MCG-finite.
proofSteps: Conjugation in the exact total-space group supplies intertwiners for the image of π₁(M).
That image has finite index in PMod(g,n); pass to the full group by the finite-index criterion.
acceptance: A local system pulled back from the base restricts trivially to every fibre, a singleton orbit.
For the universal punctured curve over a fine level chart, the conclusion is Proposition 2.1.2 for Γ the image of π₁ of the total space in PMod(g,n+1).

sources.match: Proposition 2.1.3, proved in §2.1.6, shows the fibre restriction of a representation of π₁ of a punctured versal family is MCG-finite, by conjugating with lifts of base loops and using the finite-index image of Lemma 2.1.4.

nodes.title: Finite-orbit operations
nodes.statement: Finite direct sums, tensor products and duals of MCG-finite representations are MCG-finite. Every irreducible constituent of the semisimplification is MCG-finite. A subrepresentation or quotient singled out functorially under all representation isomorphisms is MCG-finite, including the socle and its quotient. Arbitrary non-characteristic subquotients of a nonsplit representation are not asserted to have finite orbit.
proofSteps: Intersect finitely many stabilizers for sums and tensors; transport duals.
Mapping classes permute the finite set of semisimple constituents. Isomorphism-invariant submodules and quotients transport under each stabilizing intertwiner.
acceptance: The stabilizer of ρ⊕σ or ρ⊗σ contains the intersection of the two finite-index stabilizers.

Non-characteristic quotients need not be MCG-finite: in the rank-(2g+1) abelianization example U on H⊕C (C.9/unipotent-example), the quotient by a line L⊂H has conjugacy class determined by L, and Sp(2g,Z) moves a rational line to infinitely many lines.

sources.match: Proposition 2.1.1 gives closure under direct sums and tensor products and that semisimple subquotients are MCG-finite (citing LL19 Lemma 2.2.1); §8.7 uses that the socle is characteristic, so it and its quotient are MCG-finite.

nodes.title: Point-pushing restriction theorem
nodes.statement: If Γ is a finite-index subgroup of PMod(g,n+1) containing the point-pushing surface group, any complex representation of Γ restricts to an MCG-finite representation of that surface group, for 2g−2+n>0.
proofSteps: Use the finite-index image of Γ in the Birman quotient: conjugation in Γ realizes all its outer actions by actual intertwiners.
acceptance: For n=0, Γ=PMod(g,1) and the symplectic representation on H₁(Σ_g) pulled back along the forgetful map, the restriction to the point-pushing subgroup is trivial, hence MCG-finite.
The intertwiner for the image of γ̃∈Γ is ρ(γ̃) itself, so the orbit under the image of Γ in PMod(g,n) is a single conjugacy class.

sources.match: Proposition 2.1.2: for a finite-index subgroup of Mod(g,n+1) containing the point-pushing subgroup, the restriction of any representation is MCG-finite, since ρ(γ) conjugates ρ to its twist by γ.

nodes.title: Rank-one canonical finiteness
nodes.statement: For g≥1 and n≥0 every MCG-finite character π₁Σ(g,n)→C× has finite image. In particular every positive-rank MCG-finite representation has finite determinant.
proofSteps: A character factors through H₁. For a nonseparating simple closed curve a and a class x with î(x,a)=1, some power T_a^k lies in the stabilizer of χ, and LV.5/dehn-twist-homology gives χ(a)^k=1. The standard generators aᵢ,bᵢ are nonseparating (LV.5/primitive-classes-simple), and for n≥2 a puncture loop γ_j is handled through a nonseparating curve in the class a₁+γ_j.
Determinant is compatible with conjugation and precomposition; finite generation turns finitely many torsion values into a finite image.
acceptance: Check g=1,n=0 directly with the SL₂(Z) transvections; exclude a genus-zero finite-orbit character with non-torsion puncture monodromy.

sources.match: Proposition 2.3.1, quoting BGMW17 Lemma 3.2, gives finite image for MCG-finite characters when g≥1, with the Dehn-twist idea sketched after it; Lemma 2.3.2 deduces finite determinant and the subgroup det⁻¹(finite).

nodes.title: Canonical projective extension
nodes.statement: Let ρ:N→GL_r(C), r>0, be irreducible, with N the hyperbolic surface point-pushing group. Let Γ be the finite-index pure mapping-class stabilizer of [ρ] and Γ̃ its preimage in PMod(g,n+1). For γ∈Γ̃ select an actual GL intertwiner Aγ from ρ to ρ∘conjγ. Its class defines a homomorphism ρ̂:Γ̃→PGL_r(C) restricting to Pρ. Uniqueness is within the class of extensions represented by these actual intertwiners, not among arbitrary PGL extensions.
proofSteps: Schur makes the space of actual intertwiners one dimensional; multiplication is compatible modulo scalars.
Inner elements act by the class of ρ. Pull back to a fine level scheme to obtain a projective local system on a versal total space.
acceptance: If Pρ has trivial centralizer in PGL_r(C) (for instance an irreducible ρ with Zariski-dense image in SL_r), every PGL extension restricting to Pρ coincides with ρ̂, consistent with the corrected uniqueness.
On the point-pushing subgroup the extension is Pρ itself.

sources.match: Lemma 2.2.2 builds ρ̃ on the preimage of the stabilizer from actual intertwiners, unique up to scalars by Schur, and asserts uniqueness of ρ̃, which fails in general (source issue E2; the author erratum deletes it). Lemma 2.2.3 is the geometric version on a finite étale scheme cover of M(g,n).

nodes.title: Étale killing of finite obstruction classes
nodes.statement: Let M be a smooth connected complex variety, m∈M, μ a finite abelian group with trivial action, i>0 and α∈Hⁱ(π₁(M,m),μ). There are a smooth connected complex variety M′, a point m′ and a dominant étale map f:(M′,m′)→(M,m) with f^*α=0 in Hⁱ(π₁(M′,m′),μ). The map need not be finite, and its image need not be all of M, but it contains m.
proofSteps: Map α to Hⁱ(M,μ) and pass to étale cohomology with finite coefficients (IG.3/finite-coefficient-comparison).

A positive-degree étale class vanishes on some pointed étale neighbourhood of m (D0/cech-to-derived-comparison); take its connected component through the base point, which is dominant because M is irreducible.
Refine to a pointed Artin good neighbourhood, which is a K(π,1) (IG.3/artin-good-neighborhoods); there group cohomology equals singular cohomology, so the pulled-back group class vanishes.
acceptance: For M=G_m, i=1, μ=Z/2 and α the nontrivial class, the squaring map z↦z², pointed at 1, is finite étale and kills α.
The pointed form matters: the fibre over the base point must survive, so that the fibral representation of the lifting theorem is preserved (author erratum P04).

sources.match: Lemma 2.3.3 kills a finite-coefficient class of π₁(M) by a dominant étale map, through the étale comparison, vanishing near the generic point and an Artin K(π,1) open; the author erratum (P04) replaces it by the pointed version stated here (source issue E12).

nodes.title: Fibre-prescribed linear lifting
nodes.statement: For g≥1, start with the projective family extension of an irreducible MCG-finite ρ with finite determinant. After connected dominant étale base change it lifts to an actual GL_r(C) representation of the total-space group with finite determinant, whose restriction is isomorphic to the original ρ, not just projectively isomorphic.
proofSteps: Set D=detρ(N) and use the central isogeny det⁻¹(D)→PGL_r with finite kernel μ (r>0). The obstruction restricts to zero on N.

Use the discrete Hochschild–Serre filtration: first kill the component in H¹(Q,H¹(N,μ)) after making its finite module constant by a finite étale cover; only then kill the resulting inflated class in H²(Q,μ). Every killing uses the pointed C.2/kill-finite-class, so the based fibre is kept.
Compare the resulting fibre lift with ρ. Make the finite mismatch character invariant, kill its transgression in H²(Q,μ), extend it to the total group, and twist the lift.
acceptance: For r=1 the projective extension is trivial and the lift is a finite character extended to the total space after killing its transgression.
The fibre restriction of the lift equals ρ on the chosen based fibre, not a twist ρ⊗χ by a finite character.

sources.match: Proposition 2.3.4 lifts a projective representation of π₁ of a punctured versal family, compatible with an MCG-finite fibre representation, to det⁻¹(finite) after dominant étale base change, using the Hochschild–Serre analysis of the H² and H¹ obstructions. The order of the killing steps (source issue E3) and pointedness (E12) are corrected here.

nodes.title: Linear versal realization
nodes.statement: Every irreducible MCG-finite rank-r representation of π₁Σ(g,n), g≥1, r>0 and 2g−2+n>0, is the fibre restriction of a finite-determinant local system on a punctured étale-versal family with smooth quasiprojective base. All subsequent étale restrictions preserve this realization.
proofSteps: Combine the canonical projective realization with fibre-prescribed lifting; choose a smooth quasiprojective level chart and shrink the base when necessary.
acceptance: For finite-image irreducible ρ the realization can be taken on the finite cover of a level-chart universal family defined by the kernel of ρ.
The determinant of the realization has finite order, as C.2/normal-restriction requires.

sources.match: Corollary 2.3.5: for g≥1 an irreducible MCG-finite ρ is the fibre restriction of a representation of π₁ of a punctured versal family whose determinant has finite order.

nodes.title: Irreducible normal restriction
nodes.statement: For arbitrary groups G and N normal in G, let ρ:G→GL_r(C) have finite determinant and irreducible restriction to N. If ρ(N) is finite then ρ(G) is finite; if ρ|N is unitarizable then ρ is unitarizable. No finiteness of G or finite index of N is assumed.
proofSteps: For a finite N-image, the kernel of conjugation on that image centralizes an irreducible representation and hence consists of scalars; finite determinant bounds these scalars.
An N-invariant positive Hermitian form is unique up to positive scalar. Each G element transports it to such a multiple; finite determinant forces that multiple to be one.
acceptance: The finite-determinant hypothesis is necessary in both parts: for G=N×Z and ρ(n,k)=2^k·σ(n) with σ irreducible, unitary and of finite image, ρ|N is finite, unitary and irreducible while ρ has infinite, non-unitarizable image.
Part (1) is proved through the finite-index kernel of the conjugation action on ρ(N) and Schur’s lemma, without Burnside’s theorem on groups of finite exponent.

sources.match: Lemma 2.4.1: for H normal in G and ρ of finite-order determinant with irreducible restriction, finiteness and unitarity pass from H to G; the printed proof of (1) uses a false projective uniqueness and Burnside’s theorem (PAPER-LANDESMAN-LITT-24/E9, replaced in the author erratum). The proof here avoids both.

nodes.title: Relative unitary decomposition
nodes.statement: Let A be a local Artinian C-algebra with residue C and V a local system of finite free A-modules on a punctured étale-versal family with g≥1. Suppose the restriction to a chosen fibre is isomorphic over A to U⊗C A with U unitary. After dominant étale base change, V≃⊕ᵢ(Uᵢ⊗C π°^*Wᵢ), where Uᵢ are total-space unitary complex local systems with pairwise nonisomorphic irreducible fibre restrictions and Wᵢ are finite free A-local systems on M. This is fibre-constant deformation, not merely unitary reduction mod m_A.
proofSteps: Extend the irreducible constituents of U by linear realization, and use the normal-restriction theorem to make them unitary on the total space.
Define Wᵢ=π°_*Hom(Uᵢ,V); Schur and fibrewise evaluation give finite freeness and the displayed decomposition.
acceptance: For A=C and V unitary on the total space with irreducible fibre restriction, the decomposition has the single summand U₁=V with W₁ trivial of rank one.
Fibre constancy over A is required: for A=C[ε]/ε² and a non-constant first-order deformation of a unitary fibre, no decomposition with constant fibres exists.

sources.match: Lemma 2.4.2: after dominant étale base change, a free A-local system whose fibre restriction is V₀⊗A with V₀ unitary decomposes as ⊕Uᵢ⊗π^*Wᵢ with Uᵢ unitary, fibre-irreducible and pairwise distinct and Wᵢ=π_*Hom(Uᵢ,V). The proof uses Corollary 2.3.5, so g≥1 is needed (source issue E4, author erratum P04).

api.name: relativeUnitary_eval
api.statement: The sum of evaluation maps Uᵢ⊗π°^*Wᵢ→V is an isomorphism.

api.name: relativeUnitary_multiplicity
api.statement: Wᵢ is π°_*Hom(Uᵢ,V), with its actual induced A-monodromy.

api.name: relativeUnitary_baseChange
api.statement: The decomposition commutes with further dominant étale pullback and Artinian scalar change.

api.name: relativeUnitary_unitary
api.statement: Each Uᵢ is unitary on the total space and has finite-order determinant.

api.name: relativeUnitary_fibreIrreducible
api.statement: The fibre restrictions Uᵢ|C° are irreducible and pairwise non-isomorphic, and V|C°≅⊕ᵢ Uᵢ|C°⊗(Wᵢ)_m.

tests.statement: For A=C the formula reduces to the complex isotypic evaluation decomposition.

tests.name: relativeUnitary_rankZero

nodes.title: Higher Prym actions
nodes.statement: For a surjection φ:π₁Σ(g,b,p)↠H onto a finite group, put K=kerφ and let Γ⊂PMod(g,b,p+1) stabilize φ up to inner conjugacy in H. Restriction of the based automorphism to K acts on H¹(K,C), with the inverse-pullback convention giving a left action, and on H₁(K,C). It also acts on V_K=H₁ of the compactified covering surface. For each irreducible H-module σ, take the full σ-isotypic subspace σ⊗Hom_H(σ,V), embedded by evaluation; do this separately for open cohomology and compact homology. Γ normalizes the H-action up to inner automorphism, so the isotypic subspaces are stable.
proofSteps: Import the actual covering attached to K and its deck action, and the supplied singular homology/cohomology.
Use functoriality for based automorphisms preserving K, fill ends for the compact quotient, and use the generic semisimple isotypic projector.
acceptance: For H=1 and b=p=0, the compact-homology action of PMod(g,1) is the symplectic action of Mod(g) on H₁(Σ_g) pulled back along the forgetful map.
With the inverse-pullback convention the actions on open-cover H¹ and H₁ are contragredient; a convention covariant on both fails prymAction_dual.

sources.locator: Notation 7.1.1, p.35; Theorem 7.2.1 and Remark 7.2.2, p.36; proof, pp.37–38
sources.match: Notation 7.1.1 sets up the finite cover of K=ker φ, the stabilizer Γ⊂PMod(g,b,p+1), isotypic components ρ⊗Hom_H(ρ,−) and the higher Prym representation on H₁ of the filled cover; Theorem 7.2.1 and its proof use cohomology of the open cover (PAPER-LANDESMAN-LITT-24/E1 records the H₁/H¹ mismatch); Remark 7.2.2 explains the restriction to subrepresentations.

api.name: prymAction_restrict
api.statement: Restricting Γ to a finite-index Γ′ preserves both actions and their isotypic subspaces.

api.name: prymAction_isotypic_eval
api.statement: The isotypic space is the image of σ⊗Hom_H(σ,V) under the supplied evaluation map, not the multiplicity space alone.

api.name: prymAction_compactification
api.statement: Open-to-compact homology and compact-to-open cohomology maps are equivariant with the chosen left actions.

api.name: prymAction_dual
api.statement: Dualizing changes σ to σ∨; compact Poincaré duality carries the induced action and deck labels coherently.

tests.name: prym_trivial_cover
tests.statement: For H=1 the compact representation is the ordinary surface H₁ of dimension 2g.

tests.name: prym_punctured_sphere
tests.statement: The identity cover of the three-punctured sphere has open H¹ dimension 2 and compact H₁ dimension 0; these carriers must differ.

tests.name: prym_multiplicity_dimension
tests.statement: If V=σ⊕σ, its full σ-isotypic subspace has dimension 2 dimσ, whereas Hom_H(σ,V) has dimension 2.

uses.how: The theorem bounds subspaces of the full isotypic component.
Dual cohomology of a trivializing cover detects extension classes.

nodes.title: Putman–Wieland property
nodes.statement: For fixed finite H and g,b,p≥0, PW(H,g,b,p) means: for every surjective φ:π₁Σ(g,b,p)↠H, every nonzero vector of compact-cover homology V_K has infinite orbit under the stabilizer Γ of φ up to conjugacy. Quantification is over the compact homology representation, with C coefficients.
proofSteps: Use the preceding compact-cover action; quantify over surjections and nonzero vectors.
Prove the equivalent condition that no finite-index subgroup of any Γ has a nonzero fixed vector.
acceptance: For H=Z/2 and g≥2 the property asserts that no nonzero class in H₁ of any connected double cover has finite orbit; C.3/pw-small-order gives it since 2<g².
The property can fail: LL24 Remark 7.1.5 cites Marković’s counterexample to Putman–Wieland in genus two.

sources.match: Definition 7.1.2 defines PW^H_{g,b,p}: for every surjection onto H, every nonzero vector of V_K has infinite Γ-orbit; Remark 7.1.4 relates it to the rational, group-free form of the Putman–Wieland conjecture.

api.name: pw_iff_no_virtual_invariants
api.statement: PW is equivalent to V_K^Γ′=0 for every φ and every finite-index Γ′⊂Γ.

api.name: pw_no_surjection
api.statement: If no such surjection exists the property holds vacuously.

api.name: pw_coefficient_extension
api.statement: The Q and C formulations agree for this finite-dimensional rational action by base change of the fixed-space linear equations.

tests.name: pw_genusZero
tests.statement: When every compact cover has genus zero, V_K=0 and PW holds.

tests.name: pw_fixed_vector_fails
tests.statement: One nonzero vector fixed by a finite-index Γ′ disproves PW by giving a finite Γ-orbit.

tests.name: pw_trivial_group_genusAtLeastTwo
tests.statement: For H=1 and g≥2, the definition reduces to infinite orbits of nonzero vectors in standard compact surface homology under the mapping-class action.

uses.how: Convert the rank bound into the orbit property.

nodes.title: Boundary-to-puncture reduction
nodes.statement: Replacing all boundary circles by punctures gives an equivariant isomorphism H¹(Σ(g′,b′,p′),C)^σ≃H¹(Σ(g′,0,b′+p′),C)^σ. For each finite-index Γ′ in the original quotient stabilizer, its capping image Γ″ is finite index and has exactly the corresponding invariant subspaces. The covering genus remains g′.
proofSteps: Use the boundary-collar deformation retraction and naturality of covering cohomology.
Use the supplied capping sequence; boundary twists act by an inner action or the identity on K-abelianization and hence trivially on cohomology.
acceptance: For b=0 the reduction is the identity.
Both sides have covering genus g′; the printed target surface of genus g would have the wrong first Betti number (source issue E5).

sources.match: Lemma 7.2.5 replaces boundary components by punctures, giving an isomorphism of isotypic components and a bijection of invariant subspaces for the image of Γ′ in PMod(g,0,b+p+1), since boundary twists act trivially; the printed target surface has genus g instead of g′ (source issue E5).

nodes.title: Cover cohomology and family monodromy
nodes.statement: After dominant étale refinement of a versal φ-cover with g≥1, f_*C decomposes as ⊕σ Uσ⊗π°^*Wσ with Uσ finite-image unitary local systems of rank dimσ and Wσ constant complex multiplicity local systems. Its R¹π°_* σ-piece identifies, with the deck/dual convention fixed, with the open-cover H¹ σ-piece. Compact H¹ injects equivariantly into open H¹, and compact duality transfers the same subspace bounds to compact H₁.
proofSteps: Take a versal φ-cover family (IG.5/versal-phi-cover-families); apply the relative unitary decomposition with A=C to f_*C, and the finite-image normal-restriction result to its irreducible factors.
Trivialize the finite multiplicity monodromies by a finite étale cover. Use projection formula and the local-coefficient-to-sheaf adapter for R¹.
Use the long exact sequence of filling punctures and oriented compact Poincaré duality, checking the dual σ label rather than identifying every representation with its dual.
acceptance: For H=1 the decomposition is f_*C=C and the identification is R¹π°_*C with the open-surface H¹.
The comparison must be equivariant for every finite-index Γ′, which is why the cover family is refined to a finite étale cover of its base with π₁-image in Γ′.

sources.match: §7.3 builds a versal φ-cover family, decomposes f_*C by Lemma 2.4.2 into U_ρ⊗W_ρ with W_ρ trivial after a finite cover, identifies the π₁(M)-action on R¹π°_*U_ρ with the Γ-action on isotypic cohomology of the cover, and passes to H₁ of the compact cover by the inclusion into open cohomology and Poincaré duality.

nodes.title: Higher Prym rank bound
nodes.statement: For every finite quotient φ of π₁Σ(g,b,p), every irreducible complex H-module σ, and every finite-index Γ′⊂Γ, each nonzero Γ′-stable subspace of H¹ of the open covering surface in its σ-isotypic component has dimension at least 2g−2 dimσ. The same bound holds for the compact covering H₁ σ-piece. No assertion is made for arbitrary open-cohomology subquotients.
proofSteps: For g≤1 the numerical bound is nonpositive, so the statement is immediate; otherwise reduce boundary to punctures.
Refine the cover family to the chosen finite-index subgroup and use the cover cohomology comparison.
Apply H.4 Theorem 1.7.1 to each Uσ and its constant multiplicity sum, and pass to compact homology by the equivariant injection and duality.
acceptance: Reject the same statement for arbitrary subquotients in the noncompact case.
For g=3 and dimσ=1, every nonzero such invariant subspace has dimension at least 4.

sources.match: Theorem 7.2.1: for irreducible ρ of H and finite-index Γ′⊂Γ, the ρ-isotypic cohomology of the open cover, and the ρ-isotypic H₁ of the compact cover, have no nonzero Γ′-invariant subrepresentation of dimension below 2g−2dim ρ; §7.3 derives it from Theorem 1.7.1.

nodes.title: Small-degree Putman–Wieland theorem
nodes.statement: If every irreducible complex representation of a finite H has dimension strictly less than g, then PW(H,g,b,p) holds for all b,p≥0.
proofSteps: Project a hypothetical virtual fixed vector onto an isotypic summand. Its line contradicts the lower bound, which is an even integer at least 2.
acceptance: For abelian H every irreducible has dimension one, so the hypothesis is g≥2.
For H=S₃ (an irreducible of dimension two) the hypothesis requires g≥3.

sources.match: Corollary 7.2.3 deduces PW^H when every irreducible of H has dimension below g, by Theorem 7.2.1 applied to one-dimensional invariant subspaces of a finite-index stabilizer.

nodes.title: Small-order Putman–Wieland theorem
nodes.statement: For a finite group H with |H|<g², PW(H,g,b,p) holds for all b,p≥0.
proofSteps: Import the finite-group degree-square identity |H|=Σσ(dimσ)², conclude dimσ<g, and apply the small-degree result.
acceptance: For a cyclic H and g≥2, use the stronger small-degree theorem even when the order bound fails.
For H=1,g=2 the order criterion holds; do not extend the strict inequality to all |H|=g².

sources.match: Corollary 7.2.4 deduces PW^H for |H|<g² from Corollary 7.2.3 and the sum-of-squares formula for irreducible degrees.

nodes.title: Small-isotypic infinite orbits
nodes.statement: For a fixed irreducible H-module σ with dimσ<g, every nonzero vector of the compact covering homology σ-isotypic component has infinite orbit under Γ. No restriction on the dimensions of the other irreducible H-modules is required.
proofSteps: A finite vector orbit gives a fixed line for its finite-index stabilizer. The higher Prym bound is at least 2 on this component, contradicting the line.
acceptance: For a cyclic H and g≥2 all individual components satisfy the criterion, independently of |H|.
The hypothesis is dimσ<g, not dimσ≤g.

sources.match: Theorem 1.4.2: for irreducible ρ of H with dim ρ<g, no nonzero vector of the ρ-isotypic H₁ of the cover has finite Γ-orbit; it is the one-dimensional case of Theorem 7.2.1.

nodes.title: Quasi-unipotent boundary monodromy
nodes.statement: For g≥3, a local system on a punctured level-versal total curve induced from a finite-index pointed mapping-class representation has quasi-unipotent local monodromy along a suitable smooth projective SNC compactification. The same holds for the canonical projective extension, tested through its faithful adjoint representation.
proofSteps: Compactify the level-cover total space with R09.7a/stable-curve-boundary-interface: strictify the stable boundary, normalize in the function field of the cover and resolve preserving the open. Every final boundary meridian maps to a product of commuting node-smoothing meridians with nonnegative exponents.

Identify each node-smoothing meridian with the Dehn twist about its vanishing cycle (recorded Dehn-twist gap; R09.7a leaves this identification to this roadmap), so boundary monodromy is a multitwist up to finite-cover powers.

Apply C.4/multitwist-quasi-unipotence to the linear representation, and for PGL_r to Ad∘ρ̂, whose faithfulness transfers quasi-unipotence back; commuting quasi-unipotent matrices have quasi-unipotent product.
acceptance: For finite-image ρ the conclusion holds for every compactification.
The exceptional divisors of the log resolution are covered: their meridians are again products of the commuting node-smoothing meridians (author erratum P04; PAPER-LANDESMAN-LITT-24/E18).

sources.match: The proof of Lemma 8.3.3 reduces quasi-unipotent local monodromy of ρ̃ to Proposition 8.3.2 by showing that boundary meridians map to products of commuting Dehn twists (citing LLSS Lemma 2.1.1); its normalization step is replaced by a log resolution in the author erratum and in AlgebraicModuliForArithmeticGeometry/E1903.

nodes.title: Projective integrality theorem
nodes.statement: For g≥3, an irreducible unitary MCG-finite representation of rank r>0 with r²−1<g has projectivization conjugate into PGL_r(O_K) for some number field K, in the sense of the supplied reductive-group integral model.
proofSteps: Realize Pρ on the total space of a finite étale level chart (C.1/projective-extension) and obtain H¹(C°,ad)=0 from H.5/versal-unitary-rigidity, using r²−1<g.

Quasi-unipotent boundary monodromy (C.4/boundary-quasiunipotence) makes cohomological rigidity defined, and strong rigidity implies it (H.5/strong-implies-cohomological), in the order fixed by the author erratum.
PGL_r-irreducibility follows from irreducibility of the fibre restriction, and PGL_r has trivial abelianization; apply H.5/integrality-KP.
acceptance: For r=1 the statement is empty since PGL₁ is trivial.
Cohomological rigidity is deduced only after quasi-unipotent boundary monodromy is known, the order fixed by the author erratum (source issue E13).

sources.match: Lemma 8.3.3: for g≥3 and irreducible unitary MCG-finite ρ with r<√(g+1), Pρ is integral, by realizing it on a finite étale cover of M(g,n), rigidity (Proposition 8.2.1), quasi-unipotence (Proposition 8.3.2) and KP20 Theorem 1.2; the order of these steps is fixed in the author erratum (source issue E13).

Theorem 1.2: a G-irreducible, G-cohomologically rigid local system with quasi-unipotent local monodromy and finite abelianized image, for G split connected reductive over Z, is conjugate into G(O_L) for a number field L.

nodes.title: Linear integrality with fixed determinant
nodes.statement: Under the same hypotheses, ρ is conjugate into GL_r(O_L) after a finite extension L of the projective coefficient number field.
proofSteps: Use finite determinant D and the finite central isogeny det⁻¹(D)→PGL_r after enlarging the number field to include D.
For each generator the actual lift ρ(γ) is a point of the finite pullback over its integral projective image and hence is integral after finite extension. Finite generation gives one common L.
Apply the same argument to inverses, so the matrices lie in GL_r(O_L), not merely integral matrix entries with nonunit determinant.
acceptance: For r=1, ρ is a finite-order character (C.1/rank-one), integral over a cyclotomic ring of integers.
The lift lies in GL_r(O_L), not only in M_r(O_L): inverses are treated by the same finite pullback.

sources.match: Lemma 8.3.4 deduces integrality of ρ from that of Pρ and finite determinant, since det⁻¹(μ_m)→PGL_r is finite and the lifting obstruction for each generator is a torsor trivialized over a finite extension.

nodes.title: Quasi-unipotence of multitwists in finite-index subgroups
nodes.statement: Let S be a connected oriented surface of finite type and genus g≥3, Γ⊂Mod(S) a subgroup of finite index and r≥1. There is k=k(Γ,r)≥1 such that for every homomorphism ρ:Γ→GL_r(C) and every multitwist μ∈Γ (a product of powers of Dehn twists about pairwise disjoint simple closed curves), ρ(μ)^k is unipotent. In particular ρ(μ) is quasi-unipotent.
proofSteps: Since the twists in a multitwist commute, it suffices to treat μ=T_γ^m∈Γ for one simple closed curve γ; a product of commuting matrices whose k-th powers are unipotent has unipotent k-th power.

Cut S along γ. Because g≥3 some complementary component Z has genus at least 2, and Z has a boundary component η with ι(T_η)=T_γ under the inclusion-induced map ι:Mod(Z)→Mod(S) (LV.5 capping and twist nodes).

Induce ρ∘ι from the finite-index preimage of Γ to Mod(Z); ρ∘ι is a direct summand of the restriction of the induced representation (AS16 asserts more, see the source issue). T_η is central in Mod(Z), so the generalized eigenspaces of its image are Mod(Z)-invariant, and the determinant on each is a character of Mod(Z).

H₁(Mod(Z);Z) is finite for genus at least 2 (recorded gap), so these characters have order bounded by its exponent; the eigenvalues of ρ(T_γ^m) are therefore roots of unity of order bounded in terms of r and the index of Γ, which gives a uniform k.
acceptance: Under the symplectic representation of Mod(S_g), g≥3, every Dehn twist maps to a transvection (LV.5/dehn-twist-homology), which is unipotent: consistent with k=1 for Γ=Mod(S_g) there.
The genus bound is needed: PMod(0,4) is free of rank two on two Dehn twists, so a character sending one of them to 2 is not quasi-unipotent.
The constant k depends on r and on Γ only, not on ρ or μ; the application to boundary monodromy needs this uniformity only for one ρ at a time.

sources.match: Proposition 2.4 states, for genus at least 3 and finite-index Γ, a uniform power making the image of every multitwist unipotent; Lemma 2.5 proves the boundary-twist case on a genus-at-least-2 subsurface by induction, centrality of the boundary twist and finiteness of H¹(Map;R), and Proposition 2.4 reduces to it by cutting along the curve.
Quotes the AS16 result for a single Dehn twist power in a finite-index subgroup of Mod(g,n), g≥3, as the input to Lemma 8.3.3.

nodes.title: Unitarity of coefficient conjugates
nodes.statement: For a low-rank irreducible unitary MCG-finite representation integral over a number field, every number-field embedding into C gives a unitarizable conjugate representation. The hypothesis is r²<g+1 and g≥3 here.
proofSteps: Realize ρ on a punctured versal family with finite determinant (C.2/linear-realization); the total representation ρ′ is irreducible, strongly cohomologically rigid (H.5/versal-unitary-rigidity) and integral over O_K after C.4/linear-integrality.

For an embedding τ choose σ∈Aut(C) with σ∘ι=τ. Then ρ′⊗_σC is irreducible, strongly rigid and of finite determinant (H.5/rigidity-conjugate), so it underlies a complex PVHS on the total space (H.5/coh-rigid-semisimple-cvhs).

On analytically general fibres a PVHS of rank below 2√(g+1) is unitary (H.5/low-rank-pvhs-unitary), and r²<g+1 gives r<2√(g+1); transport along the family identifies the fibre representation with ρ⊗_τC.
acceptance: For the identity embedding the conclusion is the hypothesis.
A complex PVHS on one curve is not enough: H.5/low-rank-pvhs-unitary is applied to a variation on the total space of the versal family.

sources.match: The proof of Proposition 8.4.1 conjugates the strongly rigid irreducible total representation by automorphisms of C, gets a complex PVHS from Lemma 4.3.2 and unitarity of every conjugate ρ⊗_τC from LL22 Theorem 1.2.12.
Theorem 1.2.12: a flat bundle of rank below 2√(g+1) on a hyperbolic pointed curve whose isomonodromic deformation to an analytically general nearby curve underlies a PVHS has unitary monodromy.

nodes.title: Unitary canonical finiteness
nodes.statement: Every unitary MCG-finite rank-r representation of π₁Σ(g,n) with r²<g+1 has finite image, for all g,n≥0.
proofSteps: Split it into irreducibles using the existing unitary semisimplicity theorem. For g<3 the bound gives rank at most one (rank zero for g=0), covered directly by the rank-one theorem.
For each positive-rank irreducible in g≥3, use linear integrality and unitarity at all coefficient embeddings.
A representation into GL_r(O_L) that is unitary at every complex embedding has finite image (H.5/unitary-embeddings-finite, LL22 Lemma 7.2.1).
acceptance: An infinite cyclic unitary rank-one representation on a genus-zero punctured surface shows why g=0 permits only rank zero here.
Unitarity at one embedding is not enough: H.5/infinite-image-unitary-example gives integral unitary rank-one systems of infinite image.

sources.match: Proposition 8.4.1: unitary MCG-finite representations of rank below √(g+1) have finite image; the proof reduces to irreducibles, treats g<3 by Proposition 2.3.1, and otherwise combines Lemma 8.3.4, unitarity of all conjugates and LL22 Lemma 7.2.1.
Lemma 7.2.1: a representation into GL_m(O_K) that is unitary at every complex embedding has finite image, by discreteness of O_K in the product of its embeddings.

nodes.title: Formal fibral constancy
nodes.statement: For a punctured étale-versal family and a representation ρ∞:π₁(C°)→GL_r(C[[t]]) with determinant equal to a fixed complex character, if its special fibre restricts unitarily to the curve group and r>0, r²<g+1, then the fibre restriction of ρ∞ is conjugate over C[[t]] to its constant special fibre.
proofSteps: Import the abstract discrete-group relative formal-constancy criterion over Art_C: it quantifies over every truncated deformation with constant restriction to the normal subgroup, not just the given family.
For B_n=C[t]/(tⁿ⁺¹) apply H.4/artinian-vanishing to adγ, of rank r²−1<g, whose fibre restriction is the constant deformation of the unitary ad ρ₀: H⁰(M,R¹π°_*adγ)=0 over B_n.
Use the criterion’s compatible sequence of conjugators; a separate conjugator at each order without compatibility does not suffice.
acceptance: If ρ∞ is conjugate to ρ₀⊗C[[t]] by a matrix of GL_r(C[[t]]), the conclusion holds trivially.
The rank bound enters only through rank(adγ)=r²−1<g, the hypothesis of H.4/artinian-vanishing; for r²−1≥g no conclusion is drawn.

sources.match: Lemma 8.5.1: for a punctured versal family, a C[[t]]-representation of π₁(C°) with constant determinant and unitary special fibre on the fibre group has fibre restriction conjugate to a constant one, by Proposition 3.2.1 and Theorem 6.2.1 for adγ of rank r²−1<g.

Proposition 3.2.1: for 1→N→G→Q→1, if every truncated deformation constant on N has H⁰(Q,H¹(N,adγ))=0, a constant-determinant C[[t]]-deformation is conjugate to a constant one on N, by successive approximation with the derivative map dₙ.

nodes.title: Connected algebraic fibral constancy
nodes.statement: Let X be a connected finite-type C-scheme and ρ:π₁(C°)→GL_r(Γ(X,O_X)) an actual family of total-space representations whose determinant is a fixed complex character. If r>0, r²<g+1 and its restriction at one closed point is unitary, then the restrictions at all closed points of X are GL_r(C)-conjugate. This is a statement about representations, not arbitrary maps into a coarse character variety.
proofSteps: Join the two points by a chain of reduced curves and normalize each irreducible component.
Complete at a smooth point and apply formal fibral constancy. Intertwiner equations and the nonvanishing determinant show generic conjugacy after algebraic field extension.

Use that the orbit of a semisimple, in particular unitary, representation is closed (closed orbits are the semisimple points of the GIT quotient, H.1/betti-coarse) to specialize along the smooth curve, then propagate across intersections of components.
acceptance: For X a point the statement is empty.
Closedness of the orbit at the unitary point is essential: for a non-semisimple point (a nonsplit unipotent representation) the orbit is not closed and the specialization step fails.

sources.match: Lemma 8.5.2: over a connected finite-type C-scheme, a constant-determinant family of representations of π₁(C°) with one unitary fibre has pairwise conjugate fibre restrictions, via reduction to smooth curves, Lemma 8.5.1 and closedness of semisimple orbits (citing Sikora Theorem 30).

nodes.title: Semisimple canonical finiteness
nodes.statement: Every semisimple MCG-finite representation π₁Σ(g,n)→GL_r(C) with r²<g+1 has finite image, without assuming it unitary at the outset.
proofSteps: Reduce to irreducibles and handle ranks zero and one separately; realize an irreducible ρ in a finite-determinant versal family (C.2/linear-realization).

Deform the total representation with constant determinant to one underlying a complex PVHS (H.5/deformation-to-cvhs, LL24 Theorem 4.3.1); its fibre restrictions are unitary (H.5/low-rank-pvhs-unitary, r<2√(g+1)) and MCG-finite (C.0/family-finite-orbit), hence finite by C.4/unitary-finite.

Place the original and the deformed total representations in one connected finite-type family of actual representations with fixed determinant: the deformation is a path in the fixed-determinant representation scheme H.1/betti-framed, whose connected components carry the universal representation. The component-lifting statement needed when the deformation is only given in the Betti quotient is the recorded bridge gap and H.1 request.
Apply C.5/algebraic-constancy: the fibre restriction of ρ is conjugate to the finite one.
acceptance: For unitary ρ the deformation is trivial and the theorem is C.4/unitary-finite.
Outside the range the statement fails: the rank-two special dihedral representations in genus one (C.9/genus-one-rank-two) are semisimple with infinite image, and r²=4≥g+1=2.

sources.locator: Theorem 8.5.3, p.43; Theorem 4.3.1 and Lemma 4.3.2, p.27
sources.match: Theorem 8.5.3: semisimple MCG-finite ρ of rank below √(g+1) has finite image, via Corollary 2.3.5, the PVHS deformation of Theorem 4.3.1, LL22 Theorem 1.2.12, Proposition 8.4.1 and Lemma 8.5.2; the family required by Lemma 8.5.2 is not exhibited (source issue E6).

nodes.title: Characteristic socle transport
nodes.statement: For an MCG-finite finite-dimensional complex surface representation, its existing group-algebra-module socle and its quotient are MCG-finite. Iteration produces a finite characteristic socle filtration with semisimple graded pieces; no new generic socle carrier is introduced.
proofSteps: Transport the supremum of simple submodules along each intertwiner, using the existing socle universal property.
Finite-dimensionality gives strict dimension growth until the whole module; use the characteristic-subquotient finite-orbit result at each step.
acceptance: For semisimple ρ the socle filtration has length one.
For the abelianization unipotent example the socle is H and the quotient is the trivial line, both MCG-finite.

sources.match: §8.7 inducts on the socle filtration, using that the socle is characteristic so the socle and quotient are MCG-finite; Proposition 2.1.1 covers semisimple subquotients.

nodes.title: Low-rank extension splitting
nodes.statement: Suppose ρ is MCG-finite of rank r with r²<g+1 and 0→V₁→V→V₂→0 is exact, with V₁ characteristic, and V₁,V₂ semisimple of finite image. Then the extension splits and ρ has finite image.
proofSteps: Let a=dimV₁,b=dimV₂. Trivialize their finite images on a finite Galois cover, then view the restricted extension as an H-equivariant linear map from cover H₁ to Hom(V₂,V₁).

Choose a finite-index stabilizer of the actual class of ρ, as well as the finite cover and constituent labels. The image/dual subspace is then stable; stabilizing only Hom constituents does not suffice.

Each nonzero image gives a stable cohomology subspace of dimension ≤ab<(g+1)/4 in an isotypic piece labelled by σ or σ∨ of dimension ≤ab. The bound 2g−2 dimσ>ab contradicts the higher Prym theorem. Treat a=0 or b=0 and the low genera directly.
The extension becomes trivial on the finite cover and hence has finite image. Average over that finite image to split it in characteristic zero.
acceptance: A nonzero unipotent extension with trivial graded pieces and infinite additive image is excluded by the MCG-finite hypothesis, not by semisimplicity of the graded pieces alone.
Check the numerical contradiction for the smallest possible nontrivial split a=b=1 in the allowed genus range.

sources.match: Lemma 8.6.1: if ρ is MCG-finite of rank below √(g+1), with semisimple characteristic ρ₁ and semisimple quotient ρ₂ of finite image, the extension splits, via a cover trivializing ρ₁⊕ρ₂ and Theorem 7.2.1 for the image of H₁ of the cover in ρ₂^∨⊗ρ₁; the printed Γ only stabilizes the constituents σᵢ (source issue E7).

nodes.title: Canonical representation finiteness
nodes.statement: For all g,n,r≥0, if ρ:π₁Σ(g,n)→GL_r(C) is MCG-finite and r²<g+1, then ρ has finite image. No semisimplicity assumption is imposed.
proofSteps: For g=0 the rank inequality forces r=0. For (g,n)=(1,0) it forces r≤1, so use the direct rank-one result; other small ranks are handled there as well.
Induct on socle length using characteristic transport. The socle and quotient have finite image by induction, hence the quotient is semisimple in characteristic zero.
Apply low-rank extension splitting.
acceptance: The strict bound is r²<g+1, not r²≤g+1.
In genus 3 the theorem covers rank 1, while rank 2 belongs to the separate example-range classification.

sources.match: Theorem 1.2.1: MCG-finite ρ of rank r<√(g+1) has finite image; §8.7 proves it by induction on socle length from Theorem 8.5.3 and Lemma 8.6.1.

nodes.title: Finite fibral monodromy
nodes.statement: For a local system of rank r on a punctured étale-versal family of genus g with r²<g+1, its restriction to every fibre has finite image. No semisimplicity of the total-space representation is required.
proofSteps: Combine the total-space-to-finite-orbit result with canonical representation finiteness, and use parallel transport to pass between fibres.
acceptance: A local system pulled back from the base has trivial fibre restrictions.
No semisimplicity is assumed; the bound r²<g+1 is the one of the main theorem.

sources.match: Corollary 1.3.1: on a punctured versal family, a local system of rank below √(g+1) has finite monodromy on every fibre, by Proposition 2.1.3 and Theorem 1.2.1.

nodes.title: Algebraic universal isomonodromy criterion
nodes.statement: For a smooth projective complex pointed genus-g curve and a semisimple regular-singular logarithmic flat connection of rank r with residue eigenvalue real parts in [0,1), if r>0 and r²<g+1, its universal analytic isomonodromic deformation is algebraizable exactly when its monodromy has finite image. In the hyperbolic range use the mild-connection isomonodromy theorem; the unpointed genus-one rank-one case requires its separate comparison.
proofSteps: Use the Deligne canonical extension (H.2/canonical-extension, H.2/residue-monodromy): residue eigenvalues with real parts in [0,1) characterize it, and such logarithmic connections are mild in the sense of CH19.

In the hyperbolic range CH19 Theorem A (recorded CH19 gap) identifies algebraicity of the universal isomonodromic deformation with finiteness of the mapping-class orbit of the monodromy; the main theorem turns a finite orbit into finite image, and finite image gives a finite orbit.
Do not apply CH19 outside 2g−2+n>0; the unpointed genus-one rank-one case remains an explicit source gate.
acceptance: A flat bundle with finite monodromy has an algebraic universal isomonodromic deformation, defined over a finite étale cover of the moduli stack: the easy direction.
The residue condition (real parts in [0,1)) says the connection is the Deligne canonical extension, which is mild in the sense of CH19; other connections are first gauge-transformed birationally.

sources.match: Corollary 1.2.3: for semisimple regular-singular (E,∇) of rank below √(g+1) with residue eigenvalues of real part in [0,1), an algebraic universal isomonodromic deformation exists exactly when the monodromy is finite, by CH19 Theorem A and Theorem 1.2.1.

sources.locator: Theorem A, p.4; §3.2 examples of mild models, p.11
sources.match: Theorem A: for 2g−2+n>0, mild ∇₀ and, when r>2, semisimple monodromy, a universal algebraic isomonodromic deformation exists exactly when the mapping-class orbit of [ρ] is finite; a Deligne model (residue real parts in [0,1)) is mild.

nodes.title: Free-group canonical finiteness
nodes.statement: Let N=2g or 2g+1 and ρ:F_N→GL_r(C). If its actual conjugacy class has finite Out(F_N)-orbit and r²<g+1, then its image is finite.
proofSteps: For even N identify F_N with π₁Σ(g,1); for odd N use Σ(g,2). Restrict the Out(F_N)-action to surface mapping classes.
Apply the surface theorem. This is a consequence in one direction; finite mapping-class orbit is not claimed equivalent to finite Out orbit.
Handle N=0 and N=1 directly under the rank inequality, which forces rank zero.
acceptance: For N=0 or N=1 the bound forces g=0 and r=0.
For odd N=2g+1 the surface is Σ(g,2), whose fundamental group is free of rank 2g+1.

sources.match: Corollary 1.6.1: for N=2g or 2g+1, an Out(F_N)-finite representation of rank below √(g+1) has finite image, by identifying F_N with π₁ of a once- or twice-punctured genus-g surface.

nodes.title: Nielsen generators of Aut(F_N)
nodes.statement: For N≥1 and the free group F_N on the ordered basis x₁,…,x_N, Aut(F_N) is generated by the cyclic shift xᵢ↦xᵢ₊₁ (indices mod N), the transposition of x₁ and x₂ (N≥2), the inversion x₁↦x₁⁻¹ and the transvection x₁↦x₁x₂ (N≥2), each fixing the remaining basis elements. Under the evaluation bijection Hom(F_N,G)≅G^N, precomposition with these four automorphisms is the operation c, τ, ε or d of LL24 Remark 1.6.3 on N-tuples, and Out(F_N) acts on simultaneous-conjugacy classes of tuples.
proofSteps: Nielsen’s theorem (Nielsen reduction of a basis) gives the generation statement; its primary source is the recorded Nielsen gap.
The tuple dictionary is FreeGroup.lift: precomposition by an automorphism φ sends the tuple (ρ(x₁),…,ρ(x_N)) to (ρ(φ(x₁)),…,ρ(φ(x_N))), which for the four generators gives c, τ, ε, d.
Inner automorphisms change a tuple by simultaneous conjugation, so the action on conjugacy classes factors through Out(F_N).
acceptance: Abelianization sends the four generators to a cyclic permutation matrix, a transposition matrix, diag(−1,1,…,1) and an elementary transvection matrix, which together generate GL_N(Z); a candidate generating set whose image misses the sign change fails this check.
For N=1, Aut(Z)={±1} is generated by the inversion alone; the cyclic shift is the identity.

For N=2 and G=GL₃(C), the transvection sends the pair (I+E₁₃, I+E₂₃) of Remark 10.2.7 to (I+E₁₃+E₂₃, I+E₂₃), which is conjugate to the original pair by the block matrix fixing e₂,e₃ and sending e₁ to e₁+e₂: a direct instance of the finite-orbit property of C.9/unipotent-example.

sources.match: Lists the four tuple operations as the Nielsen generators of Aut(F_N), citing Nielsen 1924 and Magnus–Karrass–Solitar Theorem 3.2, p.131, and uses them for the elementary reformulation of Corollary 1.6.1.

nodes.title: Nielsen matrix finiteness criterion
nodes.statement: For N≥2 with N=2g or 2g+1, let (A₁,…,A_N) be invertible complex r×r matrices. If the tuples obtained by cyclic permutation, swapping the first two entries, inverting A₁, and replacing A₁ by A₁A₂ meet only finitely many simultaneous conjugacy classes, and r²<g+1, then the Aᵢ generate a finite group.
proofSteps: Use C.6/nielsen-generation: the four operations are precomposition with the Nielsen generators of Aut(F_N).
Although only forward words are specified, each invertible generator permutes the finite set of reached conjugacy classes; its inverse therefore preserves this set.
Apply the free-group finite-orbit theorem via the basis evaluation equivalence.
acceptance: For N=2 and r=1 the tuple condition holds for pairs of roots of unity and fails when λ has infinite order, since the operation d sends (λ,μ) to (λμ,μ) and with τ produces infinitely many pairs.
The forward closure under the four operations is closed under inverses, because each operation is a bijection on simultaneous-conjugacy classes and the reached set is finite.

sources.match: Remark 1.6.3 reformulates Corollary 1.6.1: if the tuples obtained by the four Nielsen operations meet only finitely many simultaneous conjugacy classes and r<√(g+1), the matrices generate a finite group.

nodes.title: Characteristic quotient consequence
nodes.statement: Let G be a quotient of F_N by a characteristic normal subgroup, N=2g or 2g+1. A rank-r representation of G with finite Out(G)-orbit has finite image when r²<g+1. Likewise for a characteristic quotient of a surface group under its induced mapping-class action and the surface bound.
proofSteps: Pull back along the surjection. Characteristicity induces the automorphism action on the quotient; pullback preserves conjugacy and the image, so apply the appropriate finite-orbit theorem.
acceptance: For G=F_N^{ab}=Z^N, a characteristic quotient with Out(G)=GL_N(Z), the conclusion recovers the rank-one statement for characters of Z^N.
The quotient must be characteristic so that automorphisms of F_N descend to G.

sources.match: Remark 1.6.5: the analogue of Corollary 1.6.1 for characteristic quotients of free (or surface) groups follows by pulling back along the quotient map.

nodes.title: Finite total mapping-class image
nodes.statement: For a finite-index Γ⊂PMod(g,n+1) containing the hyperbolic point-pushing subgroup, a representation of rank r with r²<g+1, finite determinant and irreducible restriction to the surface group has finite total image.
proofSteps: Use point-pushing restriction, canonical finite monodromy on the normal subgroup, and the arbitrary-group irreducible normal-restriction theorem.
acceptance: For the trivial representation of Γ the conclusion is immediate.
The finite-determinant and irreducibility hypotheses are exactly those of C.2/normal-restriction, through which the conclusion passes from the surface group to Γ.

sources.match: Remark 10.1.7: for finite-index Γ⊂PMod(g,n+1) containing the point-pushing subgroup, a representation of rank below √(g+1) with irreducible point-pushing restriction and finite determinant has finite image, by Theorem 1.2.1, Lemma 2.4.1(1) and Proposition 2.1.2.

nodes.title: Generic curve orbit comparison
nodes.statement: Let (C,x₁,…,x_n)/K be a smooth geometrically connected pointed curve, K finitely generated of characteristic zero, in the hyperbolic range. Suppose SpecK→M(g,n)_Q factors through its generic point. Every continuous arithmetic geometric representation has finite mapping-class orbit after choosing K↪C, restricting to the dense topological surface group, and transporting coefficients by an abstract field isomorphism Qbar_ℓ≃C.
proofSteps: Compare the arithmetic exact sequence of the curve over K with that of the universal punctured curve over M(g,n)_Q (IG.1/stack-and-family-exactness), using a fine level scheme where needed; generic dominance gives finite-index image on the étale fundamental group of the moduli stack.

Use characteristic-zero algebraically closed base change for the nonproper punctured curves, Riemann existence and compatible outer actions. The universal homotopy sequence and its kernel injection require the precise profinite centerlessness/exactness theorem; discrete centerlessness alone is not a proof.

The Galois orbit finiteness descends to the moduli group and then to its topological mapping-class subgroup. The coefficient field isomorphism is purely algebraic and is not used to preserve ℓ-adic topology.
acceptance: For finite-image ρ the comparison is immediate.
Galois acts through the outer action on the geometric group, and the topological surface group is dense in it, so a finite Galois orbit restricts to a finite mapping-class orbit.

sources.match: The proof of Theorem 9.1.2 maps the homotopy sequence of the curve over K to that of the universal punctured curve over M(g,n)_Q, proves exactness of the latter from the topological sequence by profinite completion with centreless kernel (citing Anderson), and deduces finiteness of the orbit under π₁(M(g,n)_Qbar) and then under the topological mapping class group.

nodes.title: Generic arithmetic finite monodromy
nodes.statement: For K finitely generated of characteristic zero and a smooth geometrically connected n-pointed genus-g curve whose moduli map is generic over M(g,n)_Q, every continuous arithmetic ρ:π₁ᵉᵗ(C_Kbar minus the marks)→GL_r(Qbar_ℓ) with r²<g+1 has finite image.
proofSteps: Handle rank zero, and genus-one rank one directly by geometric SL₂ monodromy if the hyperbolic comparison does not apply.
Apply the generic orbit comparison and the surface finiteness theorem to the dense topological subgroup.
In the original ℓ-adic topology a finite set is closed. Continuity and density therefore force the entire étale image to equal that finite image.
acceptance: For r=1 and g≥1 a continuous arithmetic character of the geometric group of the generic curve has finite order.

Genericity is essential: if a pointed curve admits a nonconstant map to a modular curve sending the complement of the marks into the open modular curve, the pulled-back Tate module is an arithmetic rank-two representation of infinite image, so for g≥4 such a pointed curve is never generic (compare LL22 Corollary 1.2.8).

sources.match: Theorem 9.1.2: on a curve whose moduli point is the generic point of M(g,n)_Q, continuous arithmetic representations of rank below √(g+1) have finite image, by the orbit comparison, Theorem 1.2.1 and density of the topological group.

nodes.title: Finite monodromy is arithmetic
nodes.statement: For a smooth geometrically connected finite-type curve in characteristic zero over finitely generated K, every continuous finite-image geometric ℓ-adic representation is arithmetic.
proofSteps: The geometric profinite fundamental group is topologically finitely generated. Precomposition with its outer automorphisms yields only finitely many homomorphisms into the same finite matrix group.
acceptance: The trivial representation is arithmetic.
Finite image is sufficient but not necessary for arithmeticity: Tate modules of abelian schemes are arithmetic with infinite image.

sources.match: Corollary 9.1.4 records that finite image implies arithmeticity.

nodes.title: Geometric and Hodge characterisations
nodes.statement: For a generic pointed curve as in C.7/arithmetic-finite and r²<g+1, the following are equivalent for a continuous ρ: (1) ρ has finite image; (2) ρ is arithmetic; (3) for every embedding K↪C and every field isomorphism Qbar_ℓ≃C, the complex local system on the punctured Riemann surface is of geometric origin (H.5/geometric-origin); (4) for every such choice it underlies an integral PVHS in the O_K sense of H.5/integral-pvhs: it comes from an O_K-local system all of whose conjugates underlie complex PVHS.
proofSteps: (1)⇔(2) is C.7/arithmetic-finite together with C.7/finite-arithmetic.
(1)⇒(3): a finite-image local system is a direct summand of the pushforward of the constant sheaf along the finite étale cover it defines. (3)⇒(4) is H.5/geometric-origin-integral-pvhs.

(4)⇒(1): choose K↪C at an analytically very general point; this is possible because the points lying over the generic point of M(g,n)_Q form a comeagre set and the very general locus is comeagre. Then H.5/very-general-rank-bound (LL22 Theorem 1.2.5) gives finite monodromy, since r<2√(g+1).
acceptance: A non-real finite-order character satisfies (4) in the O_K sense although it has no invariant rank-one Z-lattice; under a literal Z-lattice reading the implication (1)⇒(4) would fail (source issue E8).
The quantifiers in (3) and (4) range over all embeddings and all coefficient isomorphisms.

sources.match: Corollary 9.1.4 states the equivalence of finite image, arithmeticity, geometric origin and integral PVHS for dim ρ<√(g+1); its proof cites LL22 Corollary 1.2.7 where Theorem 1.2.5 is meant (PAPER-LANDESMAN-LITT-24/E19), and leaves the meaning of integral PVHS implicit (source issue E8).

Theorem 1.2.5: an O_K-local system with infinite monodromy on an analytically very general hyperbolic curve, all of whose conjugates underlie PVHS, has rank at least 2√(g+1); Corollary 1.2.7 is the geometric-origin consequence.

nodes.title: Wider Hodge finiteness range
nodes.statement: For the same generic pointed curve, conditions (1), (3) and (4) of C.7/hodge-characterisation are equivalent whenever r<2√(g+1). Arithmeticity is not part of this wider equivalence.
proofSteps: The implications (1)⇒(3)⇒(4) hold in every rank; (4)⇒(1) uses only r<2√(g+1) in H.5/very-general-rank-bound. The low-rank arithmetic theorem is not used, so no wider arithmetic statement follows.
acceptance: Arithmeticity is excluded in this range: LL24 Remark 9.1.5 records that only the relative Fontaine–Mazur conjecture would extend it to semisimple ρ with r<2√(g+1).
The bound is 2√(g+1), strictly larger than the bound √(g+1) of C.7/hodge-characterisation.

sources.match: The final assertion of Corollary 9.1.4: finite image, geometric origin and integral PVHS are equivalent whenever dim ρ<2√(g+1).

nodes.title: Residual arithmetic lifts
nodes.statement: For a residual representation ρbar:π₁ᵉᵗ(C_Kbar°)→GL_r(F_p), an arithmetic lift consists of a finite extension E/Q_p, an O_E-lattice L of rank r, and a continuous characteristic-zero arithmetic representation on L⊗E, preserving L, whose residual representation becomes isomorphic to ρbar after a chosen residue-field embedding and scalar extension. A residual geometric-origin realization is such a stable-lattice reduction of a characteristic-zero representation of geometric origin, with its specified coefficient field. Do not quantify only over unramified lifts.
proofSteps: Use the arithmetic predicate IG.1/arithmetic-representation, stable lattices and their reductions; geometric origin is H.5/geometric-origin.
State the reduction isomorphism, with its residue scalar extension, as part of the lifting data. Import geometric-origin descent to arithmeticity for its use in nonlifting.
acceptance: A lift over a ramified finite extension E with residue field F_p is admitted.
A residual geometric-origin realization yields an arithmetic lift only through the geometric-origin descent requested from H.5.

sources.match: Definition 9.2.1 defines residual representations of geometric origin as reductions of stable lattices in characteristic-zero representations of geometric origin over W(F)[1/p]; Corollary 9.2.2 works with arithmetic lifts over finite extensions of Q_p.

api.statement: Reduction of the chosen stable lattice, after the specified residue extension, is isomorphic to ρbar.

api.name: arithmeticLift_fieldExtension
api.statement: A finite coefficient extension of a lift is again a lift with the induced reduction comparison.

api.name: geometricResidual_implies_lift
api.statement: A residual geometric-origin realization gives an arithmetic lift only through the supplied characteristic-zero geometric-origin descent theorem.

tests.statement: The trivial residual representation has its trivial Z_p-lattice lift.

tests.name: residualLift_not_matrix_lift
tests.statement: Lifting generator matrices arbitrarily to O_E is not a lift unless all group relations hold and the resulting homomorphism is continuous.

tests.name: residualLift_ramified
tests.statement: The definition admits a stable lattice over a ramified finite coefficient extension; it agrees with ordinary scalar-extended reduction there.

uses.how: Tests an actual finite characteristic-zero image after generic arithmetic finiteness.

nodes.title: Uniform Jordan word obstruction
nodes.statement: For each r≥2 there is an integer m(r)>0 such that every finite subgroup of GL_r in characteristic zero satisfies [x^m,y^m]=1. For every prime p not dividing m(r), GL_r(F_p) violates this identity. Consequently it cannot be a quotient obtained by reducing a finite characteristic-zero matrix subgroup of rank r.
proofSteps: Import Jordan’s theorem: a uniform bound J(r) on the index of an abelian normal subgroup of a finite subgroup of GL_r in characteristic zero (recorded Jordan gap), and take m(r)=J(r)!.
Then all m-th powers lie in that abelian subgroup. Polynomial identities survive reduction and quotients.
Use opposite 2×2 unipotents embedded as a block in rank r; their m-th powers have off-diagonal entries m and do not commute when p∤m.
acceptance: Check the two opposite-unipotent block calculation in rank two.
The exceptional set is the finite set of primes dividing m(r); an assertion for every p is not justified.

sources.match: The proof of Corollary 9.2.2 uses Jordan’s theorem as the identity [g₁^{n(r)},g₂^{n(r)}]=1 in finite subgroups of GL_r in characteristic zero and the opposite unipotents of GL_r(F_p), which violate it for p∤n(r).
The proof of Lemma 7.5.1 uses the same identity with exponent m_r! from Jordan’s bound m_r on the index of an abelian normal subgroup.

nodes.title: Residual arithmetic nonlifting
nodes.statement: For the generic characteristic-zero pointed curve, if 1<r<√(g+1), p∤m(r), and ρbar is a surjection onto GL_r(F_p), then it has no arithmetic characteristic-zero lift in the stable-lattice sense. It has no residual geometric-origin realization once the geometric-origin-to-arithmetic descent supplier is applied.
proofSteps: An arithmetic lift would have finite image by the generic arithmetic theorem. Reduce its uniform Jordan word to contradict residual surjectivity.
acceptance: For primes dividing m(r) no conclusion is drawn (author erratum P04 restricts Example 9.2.3 accordingly).
r=1 is excluded: GL₁(F_p) is cyclic and the Jordan word is trivial there.

sources.match: Corollary 9.2.2: for 1<r<√(g+1) and p≫_r 0, no surjection onto GL_r(F_p) has an arithmetic lift, since a lift has finite image by Theorem 9.1.2 and Jordan’s theorem then contradicts surjectivity; mod-p representations of geometric origin are excluded as well.

nodes.title: Surjective residual examples
nodes.statement: For every prime p and r≥2, a smooth characteristic-zero curve with n>0 and 2g+n−1≥2, or with n=0 and g≥2, has a continuous geometric representation surjecting onto GL_r(F_p). On the generic curves in the low-rank range these examples have no arithmetic lifts when p∤m(r).
proofSteps: Import two-generation of GL_r(F_p) (recorded Jordan and two-generation gap).

An open curve has free profinite geometric group of the indicated rank (the profinite completion, IG.1/stack-and-family-exactness, of the free topological group of LV.5/fadell-neuwirth-sequence). For a closed curve send every bᵢ to 1 in the surface presentation to obtain a free profinite quotient on g generators.
Map two free generators to the certified generating pair. Apply nonlifting only outside the finite exceptional prime set.
acceptance: For n>0 the geometric group is free profinite on 2g+n−1 generators.
For n=0, sending every b_i to 1 gives a surjection onto the free profinite group on a₁,…,a_g.

sources.locator: Example 9.2.3, pp.48–49 (prime restriction corrected for nonlifting)
sources.match: Example 9.2.3 produces surjections onto GL_r(F_p) for every p from free profinite quotients and two-generation of GL_r(F_p) (citing Waterhouse); non-liftability holds only for p≫_r 0 (source issue E9, author erratum P04).

nodes.title: Arithmetic representation nondensity
nodes.statement: For a hyperbolic surface with g≥1, r≥2, the finite-image rank-r semisimple complex representations lie in a proper closed locus of the character variety. Thus on the generic curve in the range 1<r<√(g+1), arithmetic geometric representations are not Zariski dense. The unpointed torus is excluded.
proofSteps: The uniform Jordan word imposes finitely many word identities on the fixed representation scheme (H.1/betti-framed); the locus is closed and conjugation-invariant, so its image in the GIT quotient (H.1/betti-coarse) is closed.
To see it is proper, use a free quotient on two generators, map them to the opposite unipotent blocks, and semisimplify; the irreducible SL₂ block still violates the identity.
Use arithmetic finite monodromy in the smaller rank range. On the unpointed torus torsion characters are dense, so no unrestricted genus-one statement is exported.
acceptance: For r=1 the conclusion fails: torsion characters are dense in the character torus, hence r≥2.
The unpointed torus is excluded since its fundamental group is abelian and finite-image representations are dense there.

sources.match: Remark 9.1.3 combines Theorem 9.1.2 with LL22 Lemma 7.5.1: arithmetic representations are not Zariski dense in the character variety for 1<r<√(g+1).
Lemma 7.5.1: for r>1 finite-image representations are not Zariski dense, via the closed locus [ρ(x)^s,ρ(y)^s]=1 and a representation sending two generators to opposite unipotents.

nodes.title: Conditional nonflat deformation rings
nodes.statement: Suppose a nonliftable residual example extends to an absolutely irreducible residual representation of an arithmetic profinite group, and suppose its framed or unframed deformation functor has a specified nonzero complete Noetherian local W(F)-algebra R for which every nonempty characteristic-zero generic fibre has a point over a finite extension of Frac W(F), giving an arithmetic lift of the specified geometric representation. Then R[1/p]=0, R is not flat over W(F), and it is not formally smooth over W(F). No failure of the complete-intersection property follows from this argument.
proofSteps: Use the supplier’s representability and characteristic-zero-point theorem; if R[1/p] were nonzero it would supply the prohibited lift.
Flatness of the nonzero R over W(F) would make multiplication by p injective and force a nonempty generic fibre. Formal smoothness would supply compatible Witt lifts.
Do not identify deformations of the geometric group with deformations of a chosen arithmetic extension without proving the descent and extension hypotheses.
acceptance: The ring Z_p[[x]]/(p) is nonflat but a complete intersection, disproving the inference used in the source remark.
This target is conditional on a specified arithmetic residual extension and the coefficient-point theorem, neither supplied merely by the geometric surjection.

sources.locator: Remarks 9.2.5–9.2.6, p.49 (weakened to the justified conditional conclusion)
sources.match: Remarks 9.2.5–9.2.6 infer failure of the complete-intersection property from non-flatness of deformation rings; the inference is invalid and the remarks are deleted in the author erratum (source issue E10). Only the conditional non-flatness is kept.

nodes.title: Abelianization unipotent representations
nodes.statement: For G a free group F_N or a closed genus-g surface group, let H=G_ab⊗Z C and a:G→H be abelianization followed by scalar extension. Define U_G(γ)(v,t)=(v+t a(γ),t) on H⊕C. It has rank dimH+1, is unipotent, and its actual conjugacy class is fixed by Out(G). If H≠0 then it has infinite image and is a nonsplit extension of trivial representations.
proofSteps: The additive identity a(γδ)=a(γ)+a(δ) proves the representation law.

An automorphism of G acts invertibly on H; conjugation by its block diagonal action on H⊕C implements precomposition. Inner automorphisms act trivially on H, so the conjugacy class descends to Out(G).
Nonzero integral abelianization gives an infinite cyclic subgroup of translations. An invariant complement to H would force a=0.
acceptance: For F₂ the matrices are those displayed in LL24 Remark 10.2.7.
For a closed genus-g surface the rank is 2g+1, the bound of LL24 §10.2 showing that the rank hypothesis cannot be improved beyond linear in g.

sources.match: Example 10.1.6(3) describes the point-pushing restriction of Morita’s extension as v↦v, e↦e+a(γ) on H₁⊕Qe, and Remark 10.2.7 gives the free-group variant of rank N+1 with explicit matrices for N=2; invariance of the conjugacy class is checked directly here.

tests.statement: For the two basis generators of F₂ the matrices are I₃+E₁₃ and I₃+E₂₃, respectively.

nodes.title: Morita primitive exterior extension

nodes.title: Genus-one rank-two examples
